lesson.grammar_point: reporting verbs, their patterns and the stance they show (the tribunal holds that, finds that, the claimant contends that, the respondent denies breaching, rejects the argument that)

listenings.text: I've been a science journalist for fifteen years, and the most important words in any story are the small verbs that nobody notices. When I write that a study shows something, I'm telling you that I believe it. When I write that the authors claim something, I'm keeping my distance. And suggests means that the evidence is interesting, but not yet strong. Most readers never notice the difference, but editors do, and so do the scientists. A few years ago, a headline said that a study proved that coffee helps you live longer. The study proved nothing of the kind. It found that people who drank coffee lived a little longer, which is not the same thing at all. The researchers themselves had warned against reading too much into it. So here is my advice. When you read the news, find the reporting verb first. It tells you how sure the writer is, before you even get to the facts.

I check facts for a magazine, and most of my day is spent on quotes. A writer hands me an article that says, 'The minister admitted that the project was late.' My first question is always the same. Did he admit it, or did he simply say it? Admitted means that he accepted something negative about himself. If he only said it, or explained it, the verb is unfair, and we may get a letter from his lawyer. The same goes for denied, refused and insisted. Each one tells the reader something about the person, not just about the facts. I also check whether a quote is verbatim. If it isn't word for word, we don't use quotation marks. We report it instead. The rule I give young writers is simple. Never choose a verb because it sounds dramatic. Choose the verb that the recording can support. The reporting verb is a very small word, but it's where most of the complaints begin.

reading.rtitle: Final Award (extract) -- Atlântica Alimentos S.A. v. Brenner Packaging GmbH
paras: 1. The Claimant, Atlântica Alimentos S.A., contends that the four packaging machines supplied by the Respondent, Brenner Packaging GmbH, never reached the minimum speed of 120 packs per minute required by Clause 5.2 of the contract. It claims damages of USD 4.1 million, including lost profits for the four months in which its new plant could not operate at full capacity.

2. The Respondent denies breaching the contract. It argues that the machines were capable of the agreed speed, and that the problem was caused by the Claimant’s own operators, who had not been properly trained. It further maintains that, in any event, its liability is limited to USD 1.5 million under Clause 14.

3. Having heard the witnesses, the Tribunal finds that the machines did not reach the agreed speed at any point between January and May. The training argument is unfounded: the Respondent’s own engineer admitted at the hearing that the software had a defect. Tellingly, the Respondent’s internal emails of March describe that defect in detail. The Tribunal therefore holds that the Respondent is in breach of Clause 5.2, and that the Claimant is entitled to damages.

4. The Claimant also contends that the cap should not apply, because the Respondent knew about the defect and said nothing. The Tribunal rejects this argument. Knowledge of a defect is not the same as fraud, and the fine print of Clause 14 removes the cap only in a case of fraud. The claim for lost profits above the cap is therefore dismissed. The Tribunal upholds the claim in part, and orders the Respondent to pay USD 1.5 million, plus interest.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson as a realistic award extract (the case, the companies and the people are fictional)

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the extract?
choices: The Tribunal decides that Brenner did nothing wrong, because the Claimant’s operators had not been properly trained to use the new machines.
The Tribunal decides that Brenner broke the contract, but limits the money it must pay to the cap in Clause 14.
Atlântica receives the full USD 4.1 million.
